name: CELERY-BRATE GOOD TIMES, COME ON! BURGER

recipe.history:
Celery — Apium graveolens — is one of the most ancient vegetables in the human culinary record, with origins tracing back to the Mediterranean basin and the Near East. Wild celery, a bitter and aromatic plant, grew along the marshy coastlines of the Mediterranean and was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans, who used it primarily as a medicinal herb and funerary decoration rather than food. The ancient Greeks reportedly crowned winning athletes with celery wreaths rather than laurel, and Homer mentions it in the Odyssey. By the Roman period, celery had made its way onto the table in sparing quantities — Pliny the Elder described its medicinal virtues — but it was not until the 17th century in northern Italy that cultivated, blanched celery was developed into the sweet, mild, crunchy vegetable we know today. Celery cultivation spread from Italy to France and then across northern Europe, becoming a fashionable ingredient in the salads and ragouts of Baroque cookery. In America, the 19th century saw celery reach a peculiar apex of prestige: it was so highly valued that silver celery vases were produced specifically to display stalks on dinner tables, and celery salads were a marker of sophistication. Celery salt — a blend of ground celery seed and fine salt — became a staple of American seasoning, beloved in the spice rubs of the Midwest and the iconic seasoning of Chicago-style hot dogs.

Celery's role in American cooking evolved from luxury item to foundational workhorse. By the 20th century, it had become one of the holy trinity of classical French mirepoix — alongside onion and carrot — adopted wholesale by American restaurants and home cooks as the aromatic base of soups, stews, braises, and sauces. Its flavor, simultaneously vegetal, slightly bitter, and freshly mineral, became the invisible backbone of countless dishes. Celery remoulade — céleri rémoulade — crossed the Atlantic from French brasserie culture and became a beloved component of American deli menus and sandwich counters. The remoulade, a French sauce in the family of mayonnaise-based dressings, was combined with julienned or shredded celery root (celeriac) to produce a creamy, tangy salad with bright textural contrast. On a burger, celery remoulade provides both crunch and an acidic counterpoint to the richness of beef. Celery salt as a burger seasoning connects the patty to the long American tradition of hot dog and sandwich seasoning, a wink at culinary history while fully embracing the format. This burger celebrates the whole spectrum of celery's possibilities.

I confess that for most of my childhood, celery was the vegetable I tolerated rather than sought out. It was the thing on the crudité platter that held the peanut butter, the crunchy green sticks that floated in Thanksgiving stuffing, the ribs in the mirepoix that I would fish out of my soup and set aside. My understanding of celery changed completely when I first ate céleri rémoulade at a small French bistro in my twenties. It arrived as a starter in a small white bowl: shredded celeriac dressed in a sharp, mustardy mayonnaise, with capers and cornichons, impossibly creamy and tangy and crunchy all at once. I sat there eating it with bread and thought: this is the same vegetable? The transformation that proper technique and a good sauce could achieve struck me as almost miraculous. I ordered it again the next time I came in, and the time after that. Eventually I started making it at home, and then, inevitably, I started putting it on burgers and wondering why I hadn't thought of it sooner. The celery salt in the patty seasoning is an homage to that first bowl of remoulade.

The celery remoulade in this burger is cool, creamy, and acidic, and it is designed specifically to interact with a medium rare patty — cooked to 130–135°F — where the beef is still juicy and yielding and rich enough to carry the weight of the dressing. A well-done patty would crumble and dry out under the assault of the sauce; a medium rare patty absorbs the flavors while contributing its own. The fat in the patty, still fluid and expressive at medium rare, coats the palate and makes every other ingredient brighter. There is a reason that chefs who care about technique always specify medium rare for ground beef: it is not stubbornness or tradition, it is physics. The burger wants to be medium rare. It tells you so every time you cut into one that's been cooked right and see that pink, glistening center looking back at you.
ingredients: 2 eggs (1 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 large celery root (celeriac), about 1 lb, peeled and julienned or coarsely grated
1 tbsp kosher salt (for salting celery root)
4 stalks celery, trimmed and cut in half lengthwise
1 tbsp celery juice (press celery through a juicer or blender and strain)
1 cup celery leaves (the pale inner leaves from the heart), rinsed
instructions: 1. Make the potato buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture, mashed potato, softened butter, and 1 egg. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and soft. Place in oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 6 equal portions, shape into balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and let rise 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Beat remaining egg with 1 tbsp milk for egg wash. Brush buns and bake 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool fully.

3. Make the celery remoulade: Peel celery root, julienne or coarsely grate, and toss immediately with 1 tbsp kosher salt in a colander. Let stand 20 minutes to draw out moisture. Rinse under cold water, then squeeze firmly in a clean kitchen towel to remove as much liquid as possible.

4. In a large bowl, whisk together both Dijon mustards, mayonnaise, white wine vinegar, lemon juice, capers, cornichons, parsley, celery salt, white pepper, and a pinch of sugar. Add the squeezed celery root and toss to coat thoroughly. Taste and adjust acid and salt. Refrigerate at least 1 hour before serving.
5. Make the celery aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, celery juice, celery salt, lemon juice, and grated garlic. Season with white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Char the celery: Toss halved celery stalks with olive oil, kosher salt, pepper, and celery salt. Heat a cast iron grill pan or outdoor grill to high heat. Grill celery 2–3 minutes per side until deeply charred and just slightly softened but still with a snap. Remove and set aside. These can be served whole alongside the burger or placed on top.

7. Season and form the patties: Combine ground beef with celery salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and onion powder. Mix gently with your hands until just combined. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or flat-top griddle over high heat until smoking. Add patties and cook 3–4 minutes on the first side without moving. Flip once. Add a slice of white cheddar to each patty. Cook 1–2 more minutes until cheese is melted and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat. Place buns cut-side down and toast 2–3 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread celery aioli on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare cheddar-topped patty on the bottom bun. Add a generous scoop of celery remoulade on top of the patty, letting it cascade down the sides. Top with a small handful of pale celery leaves from the heart. Add a charred celery stalk alongside or across the top of the burger. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and a small dusting of celery salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
